[Section: On His mission (ﷺ) and the first thing revealed to him]

Allah sent him at the age of forty, which is the age of maturity. It has been said that prophets are sent at this age. As for what is related about the Messiah, that he was raised to heaven at the age of thirty-three, no connected report is known for this that obliges us to adopt it.

"The first thing with which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began of the matter of prophethood was true dreams. He would see no dream except that it came like the break of dawn."

It has been said that this lasted six months, and the duration of prophethood was twenty-three years. So this dream was one part of forty-six parts of prophethood. And Allah knows best.

This is the statement of ʿAishah and the majority of scholars.

The correct view is the statement of ʿAishah, for several reasons:

The first: his words, "I am not one who reads," are explicit that he had not read anything before that.

The second: the command to recite comes in the sequence before the command to warn, for when he recited to himself he was warned by what he had recited. So he was commanded to recite first, and then to warn by what he had recited second.

For he said: "I raised my head and behold, the angel who had come to me at Hira'. I returned to my family and said: 'Cover me, cover me!' So Allah revealed ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾."

And he has informed that the angel who came to him at Hira' revealed to him ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾.

So the hadith of Jabir indicates that the revelation of ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ came later. The evidence lies in the narration, not in opinion. And Allah knows best.

[Chapter: The Station of Modesty (Haya')]

[Modesty in the Book and the Sunnah]

Among the stations of ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ is the station of modesty (haya').

God Most High says: ﴿Does he not know that God sees?﴾

He also says, Most High: ﴿Indeed, God is ever Watchful over you﴾ [al-Nisa': 1].

And He says, Most High: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir: 19].

In the Sahih, on the authority of Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with him and his father, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by a man who was admonishing his brother concerning modesty, and he said: "Leave him, for modesty is part of faith."

In both Sahihs, on the authority of 'Imran ibn Husayn, may God be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Modesty brings only good."

In both Sahihs, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Faith has seventy-some or sixty-some branches; the best of them is the statement 'There is no god but God,' and the least of them is removing harm from the road. And modesty is a branch of faith."

In both Sahihs, on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was more modest than a virgin in her chamber. When he saw something he disliked, we would recognize it in his face."

In the Sahih, from him (ﷺ): "Among what people have retained from the words of the earlier prophethood is: If you feel no shame, then do as you wish."

Regarding this, there are two views.
The first: it is a command of warning, and its meaning is a statement: whoever has no shame does as he wishes.
The second: it is a command of permission, i.e., look at the act you intend to do; if it is something one need not feel shy about, then do it.
The first is more sound, and it is the view of the majority.

In al-Tirmidhi, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ):
"Be modest before God with the modesty that is His due." They said: "O Messenger of God, we are modest." He said: "That is not it. Rather, whoever is modest before God with the modesty that is His due, let him guard the head and what it holds, and guard the belly and what it contains, and let him remember death and decay. Whoever desires the Hereafter abandons the adornment of this world. Whoever does this has been modest before God with the modesty that is His due."

[Definition of Modesty]

Haya' derives from hayah (life). From it comes hayaa (rain), but that is with a short vowel. In proportion to the life of the heart, the strength of the character of modesty is in it; and scarcity of modesty comes from the death of the heart and spirit.
So the more alive the heart, the more complete the modesty.

Al-Junayd, may God have mercy on him, said: Modesty is seeing the blessings and seeing one's shortcoming, and from the two a state arises that is called modesty.

Its reality is a disposition that moves one to abandon ugly deeds, and prevents negligence regarding the right of the one who is owed a right.

From the sayings of some sages: Revive modesty by sitting with those before whom one feels shy. The cultivation of the heart is through awe and modesty; when these two leave the heart, no good remains in it.

Dhu'l-Nun said: Modesty is the presence of awe in the heart together with the unease over what has passed from you toward your Lord. Love speaks, modesty silences, and fear disturbs.

Al-Sari said: Modesty and intimacy knock at the heart. If they find in it asceticism and scrupulousness, they stay; otherwise they depart.

In a divine report: "God, Mighty and Majestic, says: O son of Adam, as long as you feel shame before Me, I cause people to forget your faults, and I cause the earth's places to forget your sins, and I erase your slips from the Mother of the Book. And otherwise, I will call you to account on the Day of Resurrection."

In another report: "God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to Jesus, peace be upon him: Admonish yourself. If it heeds, well; otherwise, be modest before Me about admonishing people."

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad said: Five are signs of wretchedness: hardness of heart, dryness of the eye, scarcity of modesty, desire for this world, and long hope.

In a divine report: "My servant has not been fair to Me. He calls on Me, and I am shy to turn him away; yet he disobeys Me and is not shy before Me."

Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: Whoever is modest before God while obeying Him, God is modest toward him while he is a sinner.

This statement needs explanation.
Its meaning: whoever has the character of modesty before God overwhelming him, even during his obedience, his heart is bowed before Him in the bowing of one who is shy and ashamed. For when he commits a sin, God, Mighty and Majestic, is modest about looking at him in that state, because of His honor for him. So he feels shy to be seen by his Friend and by one who is honored by Him doing what would disgrace him in His sight. In the visible world there is a witness to this: when a man discovers that the person closest to him, most beloved to him, and nearest to him — a companion, a child, or one he loves — is betraying him, a wondrous modesty comes over him from that discovery, until it is as if he himself were the offender. And this is the utmost of generosity.

It has been said: the cause of this modesty is that he pictures himself, during his act of obedience, as if he were disobeying God, Mighty and Majestic, so he is modest before Him in that state. For this reason, seeking forgiveness was prescribed after righteous deeds and the acts of drawing near by which the servant draws close to God, Mighty and Majestic.

It has also been said: he pictures himself as a traitor, so modesty overtakes him, as when he sees a man beaten who is his friend, or one who has been prevented from speaking on the pulpit; he too is embarrassed, imagining himself in that condition.

This may happen. But the modesty of one who discovers his beloved betraying him is not of this kind. For if he discovered someone else, one who is indifferent to him, modesty would not overtake him, nor anything close to it. What overtakes him is disgust and his fall from his eyes. Its cause, God knows best, is the intensity of his heart's and soul's attachment to him. So imagination places the other's act in the position of his own act. Especially if the disclosure between them is supposed to occur, for at its occurrence the disposition of modesty rises from him out of nobility. So at its supposition, that modesty stirs. This is regarding the one who witnesses.

As for the modesty of the Lord, Most High, toward His servant, that is another kind, which minds cannot grasp and intellects cannot describe. It is the modesty of generosity, kindness, bounty, and majesty. He, Blessed and Exalted, is Modest and Generous; He is modest toward His servant when the servant raises his hands to Him, that He should return them empty. And He is modest about punishing one with grey hair who grew grey in Islam.

Yahya ibn Mu'adh used to say: Glory be to Him who, when His servant sins, Himself feels shy.
And in a report: "Whoever is modest before God, God is modest toward him."

[Divisions of Modesty]

He (Ibn al-Qayyim, or the author cited) divided modesty into ten aspects: modesty of wrongdoing; modesty of shortcoming; modesty of reverence; modesty of generosity; modesty of decorum; modesty of belittling and disparaging oneself; modesty of love; modesty of servanthood; modesty of nobility and honor; and the modesty of one who is shy of himself.

As for the modesty of wrongdoing: an example is Adam's modesty, peace be upon him, when he fled and hid in the Garden.
God Most High said: "Is it fleeing from Me, O Adam?" He said: "No, my Lord, but out of modesty before You."

The modesty of shortcoming is like the modesty of the angels who glorify God night and day without slackening. When the Day of Resurrection comes, they say: "Glory be to You! We did not worship You as You deserve to be worshipped."

The modesty of reverence is the modesty of knowledge. In proportion to a servant's knowledge of his Lord is the measure of his modesty before Him.

The modesty of generosity is like the modesty of the Prophet (ﷺ) toward the people whom he invited to the wedding feast of Zaynab, who prolonged their sitting with him. He stood up and was too modest to tell them: "Leave."

The modesty of decorum is like the modesty of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, in not asking the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about madhy (pre-seminal fluid) because of his daughter's position with him.

The modesty of belittling and disparaging oneself is like the modesty of a servant before his Lord, may He be exalted, when he asks Him for his needs, disparaging his own status and belittling himself. In an Israelite report: "Moses, peace be upon him, said: O Lord, a need from the world comes to me, and I am shy to ask You for it. God Most High said: Ask Me even for the salt of your dough and the fodder of your sheep."

This kind may have two causes.
The first: the petitioner's belittling of himself and magnifying of his sins and faults.
The second: magnifying the one he asks.

As for the modesty of love: it is the modesty of the lover before his beloved, so that when the beloved comes to his heart in his absence, modesty stirs in his heart and he senses it in his face, without knowing its cause. Likewise, when the lover meets his beloved and the beloved suddenly appears to him, a great awe seizes him. Hence the saying: "Wondrous beauty." The cause of this modesty and awe is among things most people do not know. There is no doubt that love has a power over the heart greater than the power that subdues the body. How far is one who subdues your heart and spirit from one who subdues your body? That is why kings and tyrants marvel at how they subdue creatures, and how the beloved subdues them and humbles them before him. When the beloved surprises his lover and sees him suddenly, the heart senses the onslaught of his power upon it, and awe and fear seize it.

One day we asked Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God sanctify his spirit, about this question, and I gave this answer; he smiled and said nothing.

As for the modesty that overtakes one toward one who is under his power, even though he is able over them, like his slave-woman or his wife: its cause, God knows best, is that when the fear of that power left the heart, its awe and reverence remained, and modesty arose from them. As for its occurrence toward the beloved in his absence, it is evident, because of the beloved's dominance over his heart. His imagination deceives him about it and insists, until it is as if the beloved were with him.

As for the modesty of servanthood: it is a modesty mixed of love and fear, and of witnessing that one's servanthood is not fit for one's Lord, and that His station is higher and more majestic than it. So his servanthood to Him necessarily makes him feel shy before Him.

As for the modesty of nobility and honor: it is the modesty of a great and noble soul when there issues from it something below its rank, such as giving, bestowal, or kindness. It feels shy while giving, with the modesty of nobility of soul and honor. This has two causes.
The first is this. The second is its shyness before the recipient, so that it is as if he were the one taking, the petitioner. Some generous people cannot bring themselves to face the one they give to, out of modesty toward him. This falls under the modesty of hesitation, because he is shy of the recipient's embarrassment.

As for a person's modesty toward himself: it is the modesty of noble, honorable, and lofty souls at their being content with deficiency for themselves and their acceptance of the base. He finds himself shy before himself, until it is as if he has two selves, shy with one of them before the other.

This is the most complete form of modesty, for if a servant is shy before himself, he is all the more fit to be shy before others.

[Chapter: Modesty Is the First of the Stages of the People of Special Closeness]

The author of "al-Manazil" said:
"Modesty is among the first stages of the people of special closeness (khusus). It arises from a veneration joined with affection."

He made modesty among the first stages of the people of special closeness because it involves attentiveness to the presence of the One before whom one is modest. The first conduct of the people of special closeness is that they see the Real, glorified is He, present with them, and their whole conduct is built on this.

As for his saying that it arises from veneration joined with affection:
Meaning: modesty is a state that results from the mixing of veneration with affection. When the two are combined, modesty arises between them.

Al-Junayd said that its arising is from witnessing blessings and seeing one's shortcoming.
Some others say its arising is from the heart's sense of what one is shy about, so from this sense and aversion arises a state called modesty.

There is no contradiction among these statements, for modesty has several causes; each has mentioned some of them. God knows best.

[Chapter: Degrees of Modesty]

[The First Degree: Modesty Arising From the Servant's Knowledge That the Real Is Watching Him]

He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: modesty that arises from the servant's knowledge that the Real is looking at him. It draws him to bear this striving, moves him to find wrongdoing abhorrent, and silences him from complaint.

Meaning: when the servant knows that the Lord, Most High, is watching him, this knowledge produces in him modesty before Him, which draws him to bear the burdens of obedience. It is like a servant who performs a task before his master: he is energetic in it and bears its burdens, especially when his master shows him kindness and he loves his master.

This is unlike when he is absent from his master.

Ibn al-Qayyim's Commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 96, Verse 14 (Part 2 of 2)

The Lord, exalted is He, His gaze never turns away from His servant. However, it is the gaze of the heart that turns away, and its turning toward the gaze of Allah, glorified is He, upon the servants.

When the gaze of the heart turns away, and its attentiveness to the gaze of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, upon it diminishes, there is generated from that a scarcity of modesty (ḥayā') and shamelessness (qiḥah).

Likewise, it (this gaze) leads him to regard his own wrongdoing as shameful. This sense of shame arising from modesty is a degree beyond the sense of shame arising from considering the threat (waʿīd), and it is above it.

Higher in rank than this is the sense of shame arising from love. The shame of the one who loves is more complete than the shame of the one who fears.

For this reason, this modesty restrains the servant from complaining to other than Allah, for then he would be complaining of Allah to His creation. Yet it does not prevent complaining to Him, glorified is He, for complaining to Him is an expression of poverty, humbled need, dependence, and servitude. Modesty before Him in such a situation does not contradict it.

[Section: The Second Degree: Modesty Generated from Contemplation of the Knowledge of Nearness]

Section

He said: The second degree is modesty that is generated from contemplation of the knowledge of nearness (ʿilm al-qurb). It calls him to mount (rukūb) love, binds him to the spirit of intimacy (rūḥ al-uns), and makes his association with creation hateful to him.

Contemplation of the knowledge of nearness is the heart's realization of the special companionship (maʿiyyah khāṣṣah) with Allah. Companionship is of two kinds:

General: This is the companionship of knowledge and encompassing, as in His saying, ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Ḥadīd: 4], and His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them, nor of five but that He is the sixth of them, nor of fewer than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are﴾ [al-Mujādilah: 7].

Special: This is the companionship of nearness, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [al-Naḥl: 128], His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 153], and His saying, ﴿And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 69].

This is the companionship of nearness, which includes allegiance (muwālāh), support (naṣr), and protection (ḥifẓ). Both meanings are a companionship from Him to the servant, but this is a companionship of observation and encompassing, whereas that is a companionship of allegiance, support, and aid. In the Arabic language, "maʿa" conveys fitting companionship; it does not imply mixing, intermingling, adjacency, or separation. Whoever understands from it any of this has been afflicted by a misunderstanding.

As for nearness (qurb): the Qur'an uses it only in a particular sense. It is of two kinds: His nearness to the one who calls upon Him, by answering; and His nearness to the one who worships Him, by rewarding.

The first is as in His saying, ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186].

For this reason it was revealed in answer to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, when they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is our Lord near so that we may confide in Him, or far so that we may call out to Him?" Thereupon Allah revealed this verse.

The second is his saying (ﷺ): "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating, and the Lord is closest to His servant in the last part of the night."

This is His nearness to the people of His obedience.

In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from Abū Mūsā, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey, and our voices rose with the takbīr. He said: 'O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. Indeed, the One you call upon is All-Hearing and near, nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount.'"

This is a nearness specific to the one who calls upon Him with the supplication of worship, praise, and glorification. This nearness does not contradict the perfect distinction of the Lord from His creation, nor His being established upon His Throne. Rather, it accompanies it and is inseparable from it, for it is not like the nearness of bodies to one another. Exalted is Allah far above that, with great exaltation. Rather, it is another kind. In the observable world, the servant finds his spirit very near to a beloved between whom and himself lie deserts through which the necks of mounts are worn out, and he finds him nearer to himself than his companion, as has been said:

Oh, how many a one who draws near, claiming that he loves you,
while the distant one is more beloved and nearer.

The people of the Sunnah are the allies (awliyā') of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his heirs and beloved, to whom he is closer than they are to themselves, and dearer to them than themselves. They find their souls nearer to him; those in distant lands from him are as close as the neighbours of his chamber in Madinah. The lovers longing for the Ka'bah and the Sacred House find their hearts and spirits nearer to it than its neighbours and those around it, even though physical nearness to it is not possible for them.

How much more so for One who draws near to His creation however He wills, while being established upon His Throne. The people of spiritual taste do not give heed in this matter to the doubts of the deniers (muʿaṭṭil), who are far from Allah, devoid of His love and knowledge.

The point is that this nearness calls its possessor to mount love, and the more he increases in love, the more he increases in nearness.

Love lies between two nearnesses: a nearness before it, and a nearness after it; and between two knowledges: a knowledge before it that brought it about, called it forth, and guided to it, and a knowledge after it, which is among its fruits and effects.

As for binding him to the spirit of intimacy: it is the attachment of his heart to the spirit of intimacy with Allah, an attachment that is constant and never separates from him. Rather, he makes between the heart and intimacy a necessary bond. There is no doubt that this makes association with creation hateful to him. Indeed, he finds estrangement in mixing with them in proportion to his intimacy with his Lord and the coolness of his eye through His love and nearness to Him. For there is nothing with Allah apart from Him. If he mixes with them, he mixes with them in outward form only, not in his inner secret, spirit, and heart. His heart and spirit are in one gathering, while his body and outward form are in another.

[Section: The Third Degree: Modesty Generated from Witnessing the Presence]

He said: The third degree is modesty that is generated from witnessing the Presence (ḥaḍrah), which is the one not mixed with awe, not accompanied by separation, and for which no limit is reached.

Witnessing the Presence (shuhūd al-ḥaḍrah) is the drawing of the spirit and heart away from created things and their devotion to the Lord of all beings. He is, in the Presence of His nearness, witnessing it. When the heart arrives there, awe overtakes it and separation departs from it, for nothing is with Allah except Him. Nothing enters his mind in that state except Allah alone. This is the station of collectedness (jamʿiyyah).

As for his saying: "for which no limit is reached."

It means that everyone who reaches his goal and attains it, reaches an end, except the possessor of this witnessing, for he does not stop at any limit in the Presence of Lordship, for that is impossible. Rather, when he witnesses those heights, stands at those abodes, and beholds the Presence which is the ultimate end of ends, he approaches a matter that has no end and no termination. All ends and terminations return to Him: ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality﴾ [al-Najm: 42].

Thus all ends and terminations culminate in Him, and for Him, glorified is He, there is no end and no termination, neither in His existence nor in the increase of His bounty.

For He is the First, before whom there is nothing, and the Last, after whom there is nothing.

There is no termination to His praise and His giving. Rather, the more the servant thanks Him, the more He increases him in grace; and the more he obeys Him, the more He increases his reward in accordance with His glory. And the more he draws near to Him, the more there appears to him of His majesty and greatness what he had not witnessed before. And so it continues forever, without reaching any limit or end. For this reason it has come that the people of Paradise are in constant increase without cessation, for their bliss is continuous from One whose grace, gift, increase, and attributes have no end. Blessed is Allah, Possessor of Majesty and Honour: ﴿Indeed, this is Our provision, which has no end﴾ [Ṣād: 54].

"O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, your humankind and your jinn, were to stand on one plain and ask of Me, and I gave each person his request, that would not diminish what is with Me except as a needle diminishes the sea when it is dipped into it."

(Excursus)

What is the benefit of substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one and clarifying it by means of it? If the benefit lies in the indefinite, why was the definite mentioned? And if it lies in the definite, what is the purpose of mentioning the indefinite?

It is said: there is a wonderful subtlety in this. The ruling may be attached to an indefinite noun that has preceded, and so it is mentioned, while the discourse is concerned with a specific individual of the category, whether in praise or blame. If one were to mention only the definite noun, the ruling would be restricted to it; and if the indefinite were mentioned alone, the discourse would have moved away from addressing that specific individual. So when the category is intended, the indefinite is used, indicating that the ruling is attached to the attribute; and when the definite is used, it serves as an alert that this specific individual is definitely included. An example of this is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Surely We shall seize him by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock﴾.

For the verse, as it is said, was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. Then its ruling was attached to everyone who is characterized by it: ﴿Surely We shall seize him by the forelock﴾ specifying (the individual), ﴿a lying forelock﴾ indicating his lack of (the individual's specificity) and as an alert. For this reason, it is a condition in this type of construction that the indefinite be qualified by an adjective, in order to achieve the benefit mentioned and to make the intended meaning clear.

Ibn al-Qayyim said, after some preceding discussion:

There is no doubt that the servant draws near to his Lord, and the Lord draws near to His servant. As for the nearness of the servant, it is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Prostrate yourself and draw near﴾.

And like His saying in the divine narration (al-athar al-ilahi): "Whoever draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit."

And like His saying: "My servant does not draw near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him. And My servant continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts (nawafil) until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he grasps, and his foot with which he walks. By Me he hears, by Me he sees, by Me he grasps, and by Me he walks."

And in the sound hadith: "The Lord is nearest to His servant in the last third of the night."

And also in a hadith: "The servant is nearest to his Lord when he is prostrating."

And in the sound hadith, when their voices were raised with takbir together with the Prophet (ﷺ) during a journey, he said:

"O people, be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. Indeed, the One you are calling upon is All-Hearing, Near, nearer to one of you than the neck of his mount."
